newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rejects French Middle East broker idea.
newsitem.headline: Israel rejects French Middle East broker idea.

text.p: Israel on Sunday rejected a demand by French President Jacques Chirac that Europe co-sponsor Middle East peace negotiations.
It was already the third row to arise over Chirac's visit to Israel -- and he has yet to arrive.

"A mediator entering into the conflict -- or into the negotiations -- is inconceivable," Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told Israel Radio. "I told President Chirac the same thing when I visited France."

Chirac, given a hero's welcome in Syria on Saturday, declared Middle East peace in danger and said Europe must join the United States in sponsoring Arab-Israeli negotiations, contributing proposals and not just money.
Chirac is due to arrive in Israel on Monday.

Syrian President Hafez al-Assad supported Chirac, accusing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of undermining peace moves since coming to power four months ago on a platform opposed to swapping occupied Arab land for peace.
"Every (outside) force that will enter into the negotiations puts obstacles into the negotiations," Levy countered. "The sides are the ones who must reach agreements."

"Europe is an important element in encouraging and helping everything around the negotiations, in strengthening the economy, and we cooperate with it. As for interference in the negotiations, these are coercive negotiations. So we reject this out of hand," Levy said.
Israel was due to be the second destination on Chirac's six-day tour aimed at increasing European influence in peacemaking.

The other rows, defused just ahead of his arrival, were over his plans to speak to the Palestinian National Council while shunning Israel's parliament and to send his foreign minister to the disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem.
On Sunday, Israeli Knesset Speaker Dan Tichon said Chirac had changed his mind and would visit parliament on Tuesday.
"In the end they understood in France that they made a mistake and they're right to fix this mistake," Tichon said, adding it was unclear as yet whether Chirac would speak in Knesset or merely visit.
On Saturday, Tichon, a member of parliament from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, said he would boycott Chirac's visit.
"It's commonplace that presidents of the stature of the French president come for a visit at a time when the Knesset is in session," Tichon said on Sunday.
The French leader, seeking a peacemaking role for Europe alongside a United States reluctant to share the role, sparked the first diplomatic row with Israel even before setting off from Paris.
After the Israelis objected to his intention to send Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to PLO headquarters at Orient House, Chirac decided not to take de Charette to Israel at all.
Instead French junior health minister Herve Gaymard will visit in a move the Israelis grudgingly accepted behind the diplomatic fiction he will discuss health matters, not politics.

While Netanyahu swallowed that compromise, he may find Chirac's main message harder to digest -- that Israel can only hope for lasting security if it exchanges land for peace and allows a Palestinian state.

Arab leaders have welcomed European involvement in the U.S.-mediated peace talks but Israel has been reluctant to give Europeans an official role. Chirac's tour also takes him to Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.

"France tries very hard to enforce a balanced policy between us and the Arabs," Israeli Ambassador to France Avi Pazner told Israel Radio. He said France was traditionally close to the Arab world but had deepened relations with Israel in recent years.
